quickAnswer: Ground-floor commercial window washing in the US typically costs $4–$10 per pane (one side), $0.15–$0.40 per sq ft of glass surface, or $55–$95 per technician hour, with trip minimums of roughly $90–$135. A storefront office with 20 standard panes usually pays $120–$250 for an inside-and-outside visit, while a long glass façade on a large building can drop below $0.20 per sq ft of glass.

blocks.text: What Counts as Ground-Floor Window Washing

Ground-floor window washing covers glass a technician can reach from the sidewalk, parking lot, or landscaping using a squeegee, applicator, and extension pole of up to about 12 to 16 feet, without ladders, boom lifts, or rope access. That typically includes storefront glass, entry doors and sidelights, first-floor office windows, and the lower lites of curtain walls. Because no aerial equipment or fall-protection rigging is needed, ground-floor work is the least expensive window category and the one most often bundled with janitorial contracts. It is also the category where pricing methods vary most from vendor to vendor, which makes apples-to-apples comparison difficult unless you understand the unit rates.
National Unit Rates by Pricing Method

Window contractors and janitorial firms with window divisions use three primary pricing methods. Per-pane pricing is common for buildings with uniform, divided windows. Per-square-foot pricing suits large storefront and curtain wall glass where pane counts are misleading. Hourly pricing appears on irregular sites, small jobs, or as the basis for time-and-materials work orders.

blocks.text: These ranges align with the specialty labor benchmark of $55 to $95 per hour used across janitorial work. A ground-floor technician with a water-fed pole or traditional squeegee typically cleans 1,000 to 1,500 sq ft of exterior glass per hour on open storefront runs, which translates to roughly $0.04–$0.10 per sq ft in pure labor. The remainder of the per-sq-ft price covers travel, setup, equipment, pure-water systems, insurance, and margin. Small jobs carry the most overhead, which is why trip minimums of $90–$135 dominate budgets for single-suite offices.

blocks.title: Quick sanity check
blocks.text: Divide any quote by the total sq ft of glass being cleaned. Ground-floor exterior work usually lands between $0.15 and $0.25 per sq ft; both-sides work between $0.25 and $0.40. Quotes far above that range on more than 500 sq ft of glass deserve a line-by-line explanation.

blocks.text: What Is Included and What Costs Extra

A standard ground-floor window visit typically includes washing glass with a professional solution or pure water, squeegeeing or rinsing to a spot-free finish, and detailing frames and sills with a towel. Several items are commonly billed extra, and they should be listed in the quote so they do not appear as surprise charges.

items: Screen removal, washing, and reinstallation, often $2–$5 per screen.
Track and sill deep cleaning beyond a wipe-down, often $1–$3 per window.
Hard-water stain removal or mineral deposit treatment, usually hourly at specialty rates.
Construction cleanup of paint, mortar, or sticker residue with razor scraping.
Interior side of glass blocked by furniture, displays, or window film.
After-hours or weekend scheduling to avoid customer or employee traffic.

blocks.text: Entry areas deserve special attention. Storefront doors and the walk-off zone just inside them collect the same tracked-in grime that ends up on the lower glass. Some vendors pair exterior window service with periodic entry carpet extraction using portable machines such as the Rug Doctor Mighty Pro X3, which has a 3.9-gallon recovery tank and a 10.8-inch cleaning path, or the Karcher Puzzi 8/1 C, a lightweight 2.1-gallon spray extractor for spot work on entry mats and lobby upholstery. For larger lobbies on a quarterly deep-carpet contract, a 6-gallon, 100 PSI heated unit like the Sandia Sniper is common. Bundling entry floor care with window visits can share a trip charge.

items.name: Measure or count glass
items.text: Count panes for divided windows and measure total sq ft for storefront or curtain wall glass, noting which sides need cleaning.

items.name: Define the scope
items.text: Specify exterior only or both sides, whether frames, sills, screens, and tracks are included, and the reach limit for ground-floor work.

items.name: Set the frequency
items.text: State monthly, quarterly, or a custom schedule so vendors can offer route pricing instead of one-off rates.

items.name: Require unit pricing
items.text: Ask each bidder to show per-pane or per-sq-ft rates plus any minimum, so totals can be normalized.

items.name: Verify insurance and safety
items.text: Collect a certificate of insurance and confirm crews follow OSHA ladder and pole safety practices near sidewalks.

blocks.text: Factors That Push Unit Prices Up

Hard-water staining from sprinklers aimed at glass is the most common cost driver for ground-floor windows in many US regions, because mineral deposits require acidic treatment or polishing that can take ten times longer than routine washing. Heavy pollen seasons, coastal salt spray, and dust from nearby construction or unpaved lots also increase soil load. Landscaping that blocks glass access, narrow sidewalks requiring pedestrian control, and strict business-hour restrictions add labor. Fixing sprinkler heads aimed at glass is often the single best investment a property manager can make to reduce long-term window costs.

blocks.title: Insurance and chemical safety
blocks.text: Require general liability of at least $1 million per occurrence with your company and landlord named as additional insureds, workers' compensation coverage, and SDS sheets for any acidic hard-water removers, which carry HazCom labeling and PPE requirements.

faqs.q: What is a fair per-pane price for ground-floor commercial windows?
faqs.a: Expect $4–$7 per pane for exterior-only cleaning of standard windows and $7–$10 per pane for inside and outside. Small jobs will hit a trip minimum of about $90–$135, so a 10-pane office may pay the minimum regardless of the per-pane rate. Screens, tracks, and hard-water treatment are usually billed separately.

faqs.q: Is per-square-foot or per-pane pricing better?
faqs.a: Per-square-foot pricing is better for large storefront and curtain wall glass, where a single pane might be 40 sq ft or more and per-pane rates would be misleading. Per-pane pricing works well for buildings with many uniform, smaller windows. Ask bidders to show both if your building mixes window types, then compare totals.

faqs.q: How often should ground-floor office windows be washed?
faqs.a: Retail-facing offices and lobbies with heavy foot traffic often schedule monthly or twice-monthly service, while professional offices set back from the street commonly choose quarterly. Annual cost scales directly with frequency, so a $150 visit costs $1,800 per year monthly but only $600 per year quarterly.

faqs.q: Can my janitorial company handle ground-floor windows?
faqs.a: Many janitorial firms clean ground-floor glass reachable from the ground with poles, but confirm their certificate of insurance covers exterior window work and that technicians are trained in ladder safety under OSHA rules if any ladder use is involved. Work above ground floor typically requires a specialized window contractor with fall-protection equipment.

faqs.q: Why did my window cleaner add a hard-water stain charge?
faqs.a: Mineral deposits from sprinklers or runoff do not come off with standard washing and require acidic restoration products or polishing. This is typically billed hourly at $55–$95 per hour. Redirecting sprinkler heads away from glass prevents recurrence, and the vendor should provide SDS sheets for any acidic chemicals used.
